title: Big-O in practice, divide and conquer, and merge sort
summary: Count an algorithm's steps, turn the count into Big-O, recognize the common growth shapes on sight, then use the divide-and-conquer recipe to build merge sort and explain, with one picture, why it costs n log n.
sourceNote: Lecture 4 'Asymptotic Notation' (Aug 31) and Lecture 5 'Divide and Conquer, Merge Sort' (Sep 2) slides, HW 4 and HW 5, Project 1 spec. Real-world notes are general industry practice.

sections.heading: The big picture: what this chapter is for

blocks.md: You already know *how* to write a loop. This chapter is about a different question: **before you run a program, can you tell whether it will be fast enough?** Two lectures answer it in five small steps. Read them in order; each one uses the one before.

data.question: Is it fast enough, **before** you run it?

payoff.title: Why it matters: sorting 1,000,000 items
payoff.note: Bar lengths are on a log scale; the real gap is 50,000×.

blocks.caption: The whole chapter in five steps. By the end you can look at a sort you've never seen and say how it will behave on a million items.

blocks.md: **Why bother predicting?** Because the alternative is finding out in production. An app that sorts 100 test items instantly can freeze on a real customer's 1,000,000. Engineers want to know that from the design, before writing or shipping anything. Poon's last slide in Lecture 7 makes the same point: the math lets you 'avoid costly implementation of slow algorithms'.
blocks.label: why

blocks.body: The **number of basic steps** an algorithm takes on an input of size n. A basic step is anything that takes about the same time no matter how big n is: one comparison, one assignment, one array read.

blocks.md: Why steps and not seconds? Seconds depend on the machine, the language, and what else the computer is doing. The **step count** is the same on every machine, so it describes the algorithm itself. Poon calls 'time complexity' a slight misnomer for exactly this reason.

data.barsNote: Double n → about double the steps: **linear**.

blocks.caption: Count how many times each line runs, then add: summing an array takes 2n + 3 steps. The only thing we keep from that formula is its shape: double n, and the work about doubles.

blocks.md:
**The two counting rules.** You only need these two.

- **Things in a row ADD.** One loop of n, then another loop of n: n + n = 2n.
- **Things inside each other MULTIPLY.** A loop of n inside a loop of n: n × n = n².

So to count: find the loops, ask how many times each one runs, add the ones in sequence, multiply the ones that are nested.
blocks.label: think

blocks.title: Bubble sort's inner work (Lecture 4)
blocks.body:
for i = 0 to n − 1          // outer: n times
    for j = 0 to n − 2      // inner: n − 1 times, EVERY outer pass
        compare a[j], a[j+1]

steps ≈ n × (n − 1) = n² − n

blocks.title: Count the steps yourself
blocks.task: Run this. It literally counts the steps of a single loop and of two nested loops. Look at what happens to each count when n gets 10 times bigger. Then change the `for n in` list and run it again.
hints: Watch the ratio: when n goes from 100 to 1000 (×10), one loop goes ×10 but nested goes ×100.

blocks.prompt: A loop of n runs, then a separate loop of n runs, then a loop of n inside a loop of n. Roughly how many steps?
blocks.answer: n + n + n·n = n² + 2n. In rows ADD, nested MULTIPLY.

sections.heading: Step 2: Big-O keeps only the shape

blocks.md: Exact counts like 2n + 3 or n² − n are fussy, and the fussy parts stop mattering once n is big. When n is a million, 2n + 3 and 2n are the same number for any practical purpose, and even the 2 only matters as much as buying a twice-as-fast computer. **Big-O throws away the fussy parts and keeps the shape of the growth.**

blocks.body: f(n) = O(g(n)) means **f grows no faster than g**. Past some input size, f(n) stays under g(n) times some fixed number, forever.

blocks.term: Big-O, the way Poon writes it
blocks.body: f(n) = O(g(n)) if there are constants **c > 0** and **n₀** such that **f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for every n ≥ n₀**. c is the 'times some fixed number'; n₀ is the 'past some input size'.

data.summary: **f(n) = O(g(n))**: past some n₀, f(n) ≤ c·g(n) forever. Here c = 6, n₀ = 10, g(n) = n, so **5n + 10 = O(n)**.

blocks.caption: Lecture 4's second example. f(n) = 5n + 10 starts above 6n, but they cross at n = 10, and from then on f stays under (green zone). That's all the definition asks: one c and one n₀ that work forever after.

lines: Goal: find c and n₀ with 5n + 10 ≤ c·n for all n ≥ n₀
frames.caption: Write down what you need to show. g(n) = n, so we need 5n + 10 ≤ c·n.

lines: Goal: find c and n₀ with 5n + 10 ≤ c·n for all n ≥ n₀
Try c = 6:  5n + 10 ≤ 6n
frames.caption: Pick c a little bigger than the leading number (5). c = 6 gives us one spare n to cover the + 10.

lines: Goal: find c and n₀ with 5n + 10 ≤ c·n for all n ≥ n₀
Try c = 6:  5n + 10 ≤ 6n
Subtract 5n:  10 ≤ n
frames.caption: Solve for n. The inequality holds exactly when n ≥ 10.

lines: Goal: find c and n₀ with 5n + 10 ≤ c·n for all n ≥ n₀
Try c = 6:  5n + 10 ≤ 6n
Subtract 5n:  10 ≤ n
So c = 6, n₀ = 10 works.  5n + 10 = O(n) ✓
frames.caption: Done. Write the constants you found; that is the whole proof. (For 2n + 1, Poon uses c = 3 and n₀ = 1: 2n + 1 ≤ 3n whenever n ≥ 1.)

blocks.md:
**The shortcut you'll actually use.** You rarely need c and n₀ on homework unless it asks for a proof. To find the Big-O of a formula:

1. Keep only the **fastest-growing term**. (n² beats n, n beats log n, anything beats a constant.)
2. **Drop its constant** multiplier.

3n² + 100n + 7 → 3n² → **O(n²)**. 5n + 10 → 5n → **O(n)**. 1000 → **O(1)**.
blocks.label: think

cards.title: O(g)
lines: f grows **at most** as fast as g
Poon: the worst case

cards.title: Ω(g)
lines: f grows **at least** as fast as g
Poon: the best case

cards.title: Θ(g)
lines: f grows **exactly** like g
when best and worst match

data.note: Blue: your algorithm's f(n). Dashed: c·g(n), the bound.

blocks.caption: The three symbols are a ceiling, a floor, and both.

blocks.title: O, Ω, Θ in one table (Lecture 4)

blocks.body: Ω(n) best (sorted), O(n²) worst (reversed).
Ω(1) best (it's the first element), O(n) worst (last, or missing).
Ω(n) and O(n): you must touch everything, no shortcut, so it's **Θ(n)**.

Dropping a term that is not smaller. n² + n log n → O(n²) is right. But n·log n is NOT 'n' with a constant: log n grows, so O(n log n) stays O(n log n). Only true constants (numbers that don't depend on n) get dropped.

blocks.prompt: HW 4 Problem 2: `for i in 0..n−1: for j in 0..i−1: sum += i`. How many times does the inner line run, and what's the Big-O?
blocks.answer: For each i it runs i times: 0 + 1 + 2 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2 (Chapter 0's sum). Drop the ½ and the −n/2: O(n²).

blocks.prompt: Give the simplest O, Ω and Θ for f(n) = 2n³ + 5n² + 100.
blocks.answer: All n³: f = O(n³) and Ω(n³), so Θ(n³). Only the fastest-growing term survives.

sections.heading: Step 3: the growth ladder, and how to spot each rung

blocks.md: Almost every algorithm in this course lands on one of six rungs. Learn them like a ladder: each rung is dramatically worse than the one below it.

blocks.caption: Three panels. (1) Drag 'Plot up to n' and watch 2ⁿ and n² leave the chart. (2) Slide the input size up to a million or a billion and read the real time for each rung. (3) Race a careful n² algorithm against a sloppy n log n one and find where they cross.

rows: grabbing the top plate off a stack
a loop that HALVES what's left
finding a word in a paper dictionary
reading every name on a list once
halving, with a full pass at each level
sorting a deck by splitting and merging piles
a loop inside a loop, both over the input
everyone at a party shaking hands with everyone
trying every possible playlist of your songs
blocks.title: The growth ladder

blocks.md:
**When you see X, think Y.** This is the pattern-matching you do on an exam.

- A single `for` over the array → **n**.
- A `for` inside a `for`, both up to n → **n²**. (Inner goes to i instead of n? Still n², it's half of n².)
- A variable that is **halved or doubled** each pass (`n = n / 2`, `i *= 2`) → **log n**.
- A loop of n around something that halves → **n log n**.
- A loop that runs a **fixed** number of times, like 100 → constant, **O(1)**, no matter how big 100 looks.
blocks.label: think

blocks.md:
**What size of input can each rung handle?** A laptop does roughly a billion simple steps per second. Rule of thumb for 'answers in about a second':

- O(n²): up to around **30,000** items.
- O(n log n): up to tens of **millions**.
- O(n): up to around a **billion**.
- O(2ⁿ): about **30** items. Really.

So if a task says 'n up to a million', any O(n²) plan is already dead, and you should be looking for n log n or better.
blocks.label: when

blocks.md: **Where the rungs show up.** Looking up a contact by name in a sorted list: **log n** (it's binary search, next section). Scrolling a feed and rendering each post: **n**. Every sort built into a programming language: **n log n**. Checking every pair of users for 'people you may know' naively: **n²**, which is exactly why real systems don't do it naively. Trying every subset to pack a delivery truck perfectly: **2ⁿ**, which is why logistics companies settle for 'very good' instead of 'perfect'.
blocks.label: world

blocks.title: 1000n vs 5n²
blocks.body:
Algorithm A takes 1000n operations, B takes 5n². Which is faster?

1. Set them equal to find the crossover: 1000n = 5n² → 1000 = 5n → n = 200.
2. Below 200, the n² hasn't grown enough to beat the big 1000 constant: **B is faster** for small inputs.
3. Above 200, n² takes over and keeps pulling away: **A is faster** for large inputs, and the gap grows without bound.
4. This is why Big-O throws away constants: for big enough n the growth rate decides, and 'big enough' always arrives. But it's also why the hybrid sort in Project 1 exists: for tiny n, constants are the whole story.
blocks.answer: B for n < 200, A for n > 200, tie at 200
blocks.slide: HW 4 Problem 3: when do constants win?
blocks.slideNotes: The general recipe for every 'which is faster' question: set the two cost functions equal, solve for n, and that crossover is where the winner flips. Below the crossover the bigger constant is just a bigger constant; above it, the faster-growing term takes over and **never gives the lead back**: that's the whole meaning of asymptotic. The Big-O Cheat Sheet below has the standard growth rates of every structure and sort in one table; it's the thing to stare at the night before the exam.

blocks.prompt: Which rung: `i = 1; while (i < n) i = i * 2;`
blocks.answer: O(log n). i doubles each pass, so it reaches n after about log₂ n passes.

blocks.prompt: Which rung: `for i in 0..n−1: for j in 0..99: count++`
blocks.answer: O(n). The inner loop is always 100, a constant: 100n = O(n).

sections.heading: Step 4: binary search, the halving trick

blocks.body: Find a value in a **sorted** array by checking the middle, then throwing away the half that can't contain it. Repeat on the half that's left.

blocks.title: Binary search for 23 in 16 sorted numbers

frames.caption: Find 23. The list is sorted. low and high mark the part that could still hold 23: right now, all 16 items.
Look 1: mid = (0 + 15) / 2 = 7. a[7] = 41, which is bigger than 23.
So 23 can only be LEFT of index 7. high = mid − 1 = 6. Half the candidates are gone in one comparison.
Look 2: mid = (0 + 6) / 2 = 3. a[3] = 12, which is smaller than 23.
So 23 can only be RIGHT of index 3. low = mid + 1 = 4. Half the candidates are gone in one comparison.
Look 3: mid = (4 + 6) / 2 = 5. a[5] = 23. Found it, after 3 looks. A left-to-right scan would have needed 6.

blocks.md: Watch the grayed-out part grow: every look throws away half of what's left, **in one comparison**. 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1, so even the worst case needs only 5 looks (log₂ 16 + 1). **Double the items and you add just ONE look.**

blocks.title: The code (Lecture 5, iterative)

blocks.md: **Why is it log n?** Every look halves what's left: n, n/2, n/4, … 1. Chapter 0 defined log₂ n as exactly 'how many times can you halve n before reaching 1'. So binary search takes about log₂ n looks. For a million items that's 20. For a billion, 30.
blocks.label: why

blocks.md: **Binary search is everywhere.** A database finding a row by its id uses an index sorted for exactly this kind of halving (B-trees, a later lecture's cousin). `git bisect` finds the commit that broke your code by testing the middle commit, then the middle of the bad half: 1,000 commits take about 10 tests. Even a phone's contact list jumping to 'M' is halving, not scanning.
blocks.label: world

blocks.md: **Use it when** the data is sorted and you search many times. **Don't** if the data is unsorted and you search once: sorting first costs n log n, more than one plain O(n) scan.
blocks.label: when

blocks.title: Your turn: count the halvings
blocks.task: Write `halvings(n)`: how many times can you halve n (with whole-number division `n // 2`) before it reaches 1? This number is ⌊log₂ n⌋, the number of 'go left or go right' decisions binary search makes.
blocks.starter:
def halvings(n):
    count = 0
    # Keep replacing n with n // 2 while n is bigger than 1.
    # Add 1 to count each time you halve.
    return count

for n in [1, 2, 16, 1000, 1_000_000]:
    print(f"{n:>9,} -> {halvings(n)}")
blocks.check:
assert halvings(1) == 0, "halvings(1) should be 0: 1 is already 1, nothing to halve."
assert halvings(2) == 1, "halvings(2) should be 1: 2 → 1."
assert halvings(16) == 4, "halvings(16) should be 4: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1."
assert halvings(1000) == 9, "halvings(1000) should be 9: 1000 → 500 → 250 → 125 → 62 → 31 → 15 → 7 → 3 → 1."
assert halvings(1_000_000) == 19, "halvings(1,000,000) should be 19. Are you stopping when n reaches 1?"
hints: Use a `while n > 1:` loop.
Inside the loop: `n = n // 2` and `count += 1`.
Return count after the loop ends.
blocks.success: A million items, 19 halvings. That's why binary search on a million sorted items needs only about 20 comparisons.

blocks.prompt: A sorted array has 1,024 items. At most how many 'go left or right' decisions does binary search make?
blocks.answer: log₂ 1024 = 10 halvings (plus one final look at the last candidate).

sections.heading: Step 5: divide and conquer, a recipe

blocks.body: A recipe for designing algorithms in three steps: **divide** the problem into smaller copies of the same problem, **conquer** each copy by solving it the same way (recursion), and **combine** the answers.

frames.caption: The problem: sort these 8 numbers. Too many to do in one go, so use the recipe.
1 · DIVIDE: cut it into two smaller copies of the same problem: [7, 3, 9, 1] and [4, 8, 2, 6].
2 · CONQUER: solve each half the same way (recursion). Now each half is sorted: [1, 3, 7, 9] and [2, 4, 6, 8].
3 · COMBINE: merge the two sorted halves into the answer, [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9]. For merge sort, this step is where the work is.

blocks.body: The size where you stop dividing because the answer is obvious. For sorting: one item (or zero) is already sorted. Without a base case, the recursion never stops.

blocks.md: Recursion can feel circular: how can a function use itself? The answer is that every call works on a **smaller** input, so the calls must eventually hit the base case, which answers without calling again. Then each call hands its answer back to the one that called it.

**How to design with it.** Ask three questions: (1) If a friend handed me the answers for each half, could I build the full answer quickly? (2) What's the smallest input where the answer is obvious? (3) Does splitting really shrink the problem? If all three are yes, divide and conquer will work.
blocks.label: think

blocks.md: **At company scale.** Google's MapReduce, the idea behind processing the whole web, is divide and conquer: split the data across thousands of machines (divide), let each work alone (conquer), gather the results (combine). The same pattern runs sorting of files too big for memory: sort chunks that fit, then merge the sorted chunks. Your phone's photo app making thumbnails on every CPU core at once is the same idea on a small scale.
blocks.label: world

blocks.body: **Poon's definition** **Divide**: break the problem into smaller subproblems that are the same kind of problem as the original. **Conquer**: solve them recursively; when a subproblem is small enough (the **base case**), solve it directly. Many algorithms add a third step, **combine**: put the sub-answers together. His examples: binary search and dictionary lookup.

blocks.prompt: In binary search, what are divide, conquer, and combine?
blocks.answer: Divide: compare with the middle. Conquer: search the one half that can hold the target. Combine: nothing, the answer from that half is the answer.

sections.heading: Merge: the one move merge sort needs

blocks.body: Take **two sorted lists** and produce **one sorted list** containing everything from both, by repeatedly taking the smaller of the two front items.

blocks.md: **Why merging is easy but sorting is hard.** In two sorted piles, the smallest item overall must be on the front of one pile: nothing buried can be smaller than the front of its own pile. So you never search. You just compare two fronts, take the smaller, and repeat. Each step places one item for good.
blocks.label: why

frames.caption: Two sorted piles and an empty output. Finger i is on the left pile's front, j on the right pile's front, k on the next output slot.
Compare the two fronts: 2 vs 3. The smaller one, 2, is the smallest item left anywhere.
2 moves to the output. Only that pile's finger moves forward.
Compare the two fronts: 5 vs 3. The smaller one, 3, is the smallest item left anywhere.
3 moves to the output. Only that pile's finger moves forward.
Compare the two fronts: 5 vs 6. The smaller one, 5, is the smallest item left anywhere.
5 moves to the output. Only that pile's finger moves forward.
Compare the two fronts: 8 vs 6. The smaller one, 6, is the smallest item left anywhere.
6 moves to the output. Only that pile's finger moves forward.
Compare the two fronts: 8 vs 9. The smaller one, 8, is the smallest item left anywhere.
8 moves to the output. Only that pile's finger moves forward.
Compare the two fronts: 12 vs 9. The smaller one, 9, is the smallest item left anywhere.
9 moves to the output. Only that pile's finger moves forward.
Compare the two fronts: 12 vs 10. The smaller one, 10, is the smallest item left anywhere.
10 moves to the output. Only that pile's finger moves forward.
The other pile ran out, so the rest of the left pile is copied down in order, no comparisons needed. Every item was copied exactly once: 8 copies, O(n).

blocks.md: **Cost of one merge.** Every step copies one item to the output, and nothing is copied twice. Merging lists with n items in total therefore takes about **n steps: O(n)**.

blocks.title: This is the shape Project 1 needs: it merges a[lo..mid] with a[mid+1..hi] into tmp, then copies back. `i` and `j` are the two fingers; `k` is the output position.
blocks.slide: merge in Java, working on a subrange with a temp array

blocks.md: **Merging sorted lists is a daily job for software.** Your email app showing messages from several accounts in one timeline is merging lists already sorted by date. A database answering 'join these two tables' often sorts both and merges them (a 'merge join'). Version control tools merge ordered sequences of lines. When data is already sorted, merging is the cheapest way to combine it.
blocks.label: world

blocks.title: Your turn: write merge
blocks.task: Finish the loop so it compares `left[i]` and `right[j]`, appends the smaller one to `out`, and moves that finger forward. Delete the `break` line when you write your version. Use `<=` so ties take from the left (that keeps merge sort stable).
blocks.starter:
def merge(left, right):
    out = []
    i, j = 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        # compare left[i] and right[j], append the smaller one,
        # then move that finger (i += 1 or j += 1)
        break   # delete this line once your comparison is written
    # one pile ran out: copy whatever is left of both
    out.extend(left[i:])
    out.extend(right[j:])
    return out

print(merge([2, 5, 8, 12], [3, 6, 9, 10]))
blocks.check:
r = merge([2, 5, 8, 12], [3, 6, 9, 10])
assert r == [2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12], f"merge([2, 5, 8, 12], [3, 6, 9, 10]) gave {r}. Did you compare left[i] with right[j] and move only one finger?"
assert merge([], [1, 2]) == [1, 2], "Merging with an empty list should give the other list back."
assert merge([1, 4], []) == [1, 4], "Merging with an empty list should give the other list back."
assert merge([1, 1, 3], [1, 2]) == [1, 1, 1, 2, 3], "Ties: equal values should all end up in the output."
assert merge([10], [1, 2, 3]) == [1, 2, 3, 10], "One pile can run out long before the other."
blocks.solution:
def merge(left, right):
    out = []
    i, j = 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            out.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            out.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    out.extend(left[i:])
    out.extend(right[j:])
    return out

print(merge([2, 5, 8, 12], [3, 6, 9, 10]))
hints: Use an if/else: `if left[i] <= right[j]:` take from the left, else take from the right.
In the left branch: `out.append(left[i])` then `i += 1`.
In the right branch: `out.append(right[j])` then `j += 1`. Don't forget to delete the `break`.
blocks.success: That's the heart of merge sort, and the same merge the Java version in Project 1 needs.

blocks.prompt: Merging [1, 4, 9] with [2, 3, 10, 11]: how many comparisons happen before one list runs out?
blocks.answer: 1v2 take 1; 4v2 take 2; 4v3 take 3; 4v10 take 4; 9v10 take 9. The left list is now empty: 5 comparisons. Then 10, 11 are copied with no comparisons.

blocks.body: Split the array in half, merge-sort each half, then **merge** the two sorted halves. A piece of size 1 is already sorted (the base case).

blocks.title: Merge sort on [50, 20, 60, 30, 10]: split down, merge up

frames.caption: Merge sort on [50, 20, 60, 30, 10]. Going DOWN it only splits; there are no comparisons yet.
Split every piece in the middle (the left half gets the extra item). A piece of size 1 stops: it's already sorted.
Split every piece in the middle (the left half gets the extra item). A piece of size 1 stops: it's already sorted.
Every piece is size 1: the base case. Now the real work starts, coming back UP.
Merge each pair of sorted neighbors: [20, 50]. Every comparison merge sort makes happens here, on the way up.
Merge each pair of sorted neighbors: [20, 50, 60], [10, 30]. Every comparison merge sort makes happens here, on the way up.
The last merge: [10, 20, 30, 50, 60]. Sorted. 3 levels of merging, each touching all 5 items: about n log n work.

blocks.md: Merge sort is an hourglass. Going **down** it only cuts (no comparisons at all). Coming **up** it merges, and every comparison in the whole algorithm happens on the way up.

blocks.md: **How to trace merge sort without getting lost.** Always finish the LEFT side completely before touching the right. Write each call on its own line, indented by depth; write → result only after both of its children have returned. Odd length: the left half gets the extra item (mid = (lo + hi) / 2).

sections.heading: Why merge sort costs n log n (one picture)

blocks.md: This is the most important picture of the first half of the course. It comes back in Lecture 6 (recurrences), Lecture 7 (the master method), Lecture 8 (heap sort) and Lecture 9 (quicksort's best case).

data.summary: n per level × log₂ n levels = **n log n**

blocks.caption: Every level's merges handle each item once, so every level costs n. There are log₂ n levels of merging, because that's how many halvings get you from n to 1.
blocks.slide: n per level × log n levels

lines: 1. One level's merges touch every item once: n steps
frames.caption: No matter how many pieces a level is cut into, together they hold all n items, and merging touches each item once.

lines: 1. One level's merges touch every item once: n steps
2. The sizes go n, n/2, n/4, …, 1: log₂ n levels
frames.caption: Chapter 0: the number of halvings from n to 1 is log₂ n.

lines: 1. One level's merges touch every item once: n steps
2. The sizes go n, n/2, n/4, …, 1: log₂ n levels
3. Splitting is free (just compute mid): O(n) total
frames.caption: Poon counts n − 1 splits, each O(1). That's O(n), which is smaller than what the merges cost.

lines: 1. One level's merges touch every item once: n steps
2. The sizes go n, n/2, n/4, …, 1: log₂ n levels
3. Splitting is free (just compute mid): O(n) total
4. Total: n × log n + n = O(n log n)
frames.caption: Keep the biggest term. Merge sort is O(n log n), and since it does this work on every input, even sorted input, it's Θ(n log n).

blocks.md: n = 1,000,000. Merge sort: about n log n = 1,000,000 × 20 = 20,000,000 operations. Insertion sort worst case: about n² = 10¹². That's the difference between a blink and eleven days. This is the sentence to remember when someone asks why growth rate matters more than constants.

blocks.title: See it: count the comparisons
blocks.task: This runs merge sort and insertion sort on random lists of growing size, counts their comparisons, and plots both. Run it. Insertion sort's curve bends upward (n²); merge sort's stays nearly straight (n log n). Try adding 1600 to `sizes`.
blocks.starter:
import random, math
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def merge_sort_count(a):
    """Sort a; return (sorted list, number of comparisons)."""
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a, 0
    mid = (len(a) + 1) // 2          # left half gets the extra item
    left, cl = merge_sort_count(a[:mid])
    right, cr = merge_sort_count(a[mid:])
    out, i, j, c = [], 0, 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        c += 1
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            out.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            out.append(right[j]); j += 1
    return out + left[i:] + right[j:], cl + cr + c

def insertion_sort_count(a):
    a, c = a[:], 0
    for j in range(1, len(a)):
        key, i = a[j], j - 1
        while i >= 0:
            c += 1
            if a[i] > key:
                a[i + 1] = a[i]; i -= 1
            else:
                break
        a[i + 1] = key
    return a, c

sizes = [10, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800]
ms, ins = [], []
for n in sizes:
    data = [random.random() for _ in range(n)]
    ms.append(merge_sort_count(data)[1])
    ins.append(insertion_sort_count(data)[1])
    print(f"n = {n:4}: merge {ms[-1]:6,}   insertion {ins[-1]:7,}   n·log2(n) = {round(n * math.log2(n)):6,}")

plt.plot(sizes, ins, "o-", label="insertion sort (about n²/4 on random input)")
plt.plot(sizes, ms, "o-", label="merge sort (about n log n)")
plt.xlabel("n (items)"); plt.ylabel("comparisons"); plt.legend(); plt.title("Comparisons on random input")
plt.show()

blocks.prompt: Merge sort on n = 16: how many levels of merging, and about how many item-moves in total?
blocks.answer: log₂ 16 = 4 levels, 16 moves per level: about 64.

blocks.prompt: Why is merge sort O(n log n) even in the best case, when insertion sort can be Ω(n)?
blocks.answer: Merge sort always makes the same splits and always merges every level; it never notices that the input was sorted. Insertion sort's inner loop stops early on sorted input, so it does less work.

rows: n is tiny or nearly sorted

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **O(n) space: the price of the speed** Merge writes its output somewhere. If it wrote straight back into the input array, it would overwrite elements it hasn't read yet: merging [2, 5] with [1, 4] in place, the 1 has to go where the 2 is, but the 2 hasn't been placed yet. So merge needs a temporary array the size of the input: **O(n) extra space**. Slide 38 walks through exactly this. Heap sort (Lecture 8) is the sort that avoids it.
blocks.slide: Why merge sort needs extra space

blocks.md:
**Pick insertion sort** when the list is tiny (under a few dozen items) or already almost sorted, like adding one new score to a sorted leaderboard: it does almost no work then, and it needs no extra memory.

**Pick merge sort** when the list is big, when you need a guaranteed n log n no matter what the input looks like, when equal items must keep their order (stable), or when the data doesn't fit in memory and must be merged from disk.

**Watch out for** merge sort's extra O(n) memory on small devices. Heap sort (Lecture 8) fixes that.
blocks.label: when

blocks.md: **The real answer is 'both'.** Python's built-in sort and Java's sort for objects use **Timsort**: it finds runs that are already sorted, uses insertion sort to extend short runs, and merges runs merge-sort style. That's exactly Project 1's hybrid sort idea, used by billions of devices. Real-world data is often partly sorted, and this hybrid takes advantage of it.
blocks.label: world

blocks.body: Saying merge sort sorts 'in place'. It doesn't: merge writes into a temporary array of size n, so it uses O(n) extra space. Insertion sort (and later heap sort) are the in-place ones.

Part 2 runs the provided `main()` to time them and asks you to write about what you see. Everything above in this chapter and the previous one *is* the project; the code blocks here are the pieces. Check the spec for the exact method names and signatures he expects, and use his: he docks for format.

blocks.title: Words from this chapter

exercises.title: Spot the rung: halving
exercises.prompt: What is the Big-O of this loop?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: i takes the values n, n/2, n/4, …, 2.
The number of halvings from n to 1 is log₂ n.
So the loop body runs about log₂ n times: O(log n).
exercises.why: Halving loops are the fingerprint of log n: binary search, heap operations, and the height of merge sort's tree.

choices.feedback: It depends on n: bigger n means more passes.
Right. i is halved each pass, so there are about log₂ n passes.
It doesn't visit every value from n down to 1; it jumps by halving.
O(n/2) would be a loop that goes down by 1 until n/2. And n/2 is just O(n) anyway.

exercises.title: Spot the rung: a constant inner loop
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: The outer loop runs n times.
The inner loop runs 50 times every time: a constant.
50n → drop the constant → O(n).
exercises.why: Only loops whose length depends on n change the rung. This is a common exam trick.

choices.feedback: Nested loops multiply, but the inner one is 50, not n.
The inner loop never depends on n, and constants are dropped anyway.
Right: 50 × n = 50n = O(n).
The outer loop grows with n.

exercises.title: Keep the fastest term
exercises.prompt: Give the Big-O of T(n) = 4n² + 300n log n + 10⁶. Answer like O(n^2).
hints: Which of the three terms grows fastest as n gets huge?
n² beats n log n (because n beats log n), and both beat a constant.
Keep 4n², drop the 4.
solution: Terms: 4n², 300 n log n, 10⁶.
Fastest-growing: n².
Drop the constant 4: O(n²).
exercises.why: Big constants like 300 or 10⁶ feel important, but for big enough n the shape always wins.

exercises.title: Find c
exercises.prompt: To prove 3n + 8 = O(n) with n₀ = 8, what is the smallest whole-number c that works? (We need 3n + 8 ≤ c·n for all n ≥ 8.)
hints: Try c = 4: is 3n + 8 ≤ 4n when n ≥ 8?
3n + 8 ≤ 4n ⟺ 8 ≤ n. True for all n ≥ 8.
Could c = 3 work? 3n + 8 ≤ 3n means 8 ≤ 0: never.
solution: c = 3 fails: 3n + 8 ≤ 3n is never true.
c = 4: 3n + 8 ≤ 4n ⟺ n ≥ 8. True from n₀ = 8 on.
So c = 4.
exercises.why: This is the exact pattern of Poon's 5n + 10 example: one more than the leading number, and n₀ equal to the constant.

exercises.title: Binary search looks
exercises.prompt: About how many halvings does binary search need on a sorted list of 1,000,000 items? (Give the whole number of times you can halve 1,000,000 before reaching 1.)
hints: Halving with whole numbers stops after 19; counting the final look it's 20.
solution: About 19 to 20 looks, compared with up to 1,000,000 for a linear scan.
exercises.why: This is why databases and search indexes keep data sorted: lookups stay tiny even when the data is enormous.

exercises.title: Cost of a merge
exercises.prompt: Merging two sorted lists of 500 items each takes how many steps, roughly?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: Each step copies one item into the output.
No item is copied twice.
1,000 items total → about 1,000 steps.
exercises.why: Merge is linear because sortedness lets you skip searching. That single fact is where merge sort's speed comes from.

choices.feedback: That's the number of halvings, not of copies.
Right: every item is copied to the output exactly once, so about 1,000 steps: O(n).
That's (n/2)², what you'd get comparing every pair. Merge never does that.
That's n², far too many.

exercises.title: Where merge sort does its work
exercises.prompt: In merge sort, where do the comparisons between items actually happen?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: Going down: just cutting.
Base case: one item, nothing to do.
Coming up: merge compares fronts. That's all the work.
exercises.why: Quicksort (Lecture 9) is the mirror image: all its work happens on the way DOWN (partition), and there is nothing to combine.

choices.text: While splitting the array in half
choices.feedback: Splitting just computes mid = (lo + hi) / 2. No item is looked at.
A single item needs no comparison: it's already sorted.

choices.text: While merging, on the way back up
choices.feedback: Right. All comparisons happen in merge, as the recursion returns.
It's a comparison sort: merge compares two fronts.

exercises.title: Pick the sort
exercises.prompt: A fitness app keeps a leaderboard of 5,000 scores, always sorted. Each minute, one new score arrives and must be put in place. Which is the better fit?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: The list is already sorted except one item.
Insertion sort's best case is on nearly sorted input.
Sliding one item into place is at most n shifts.
exercises.why: Matching the algorithm to the shape of the data, not just its size, is what real engineers do. It's also why Timsort looks for already-sorted runs.

choices.text: Merge sort the whole list each minute
choices.feedback: That's n log n ≈ 60,000 steps every minute to place one item.

choices.text: Insertion sort's idea: slide the new score into place
choices.feedback: Right. On an almost-sorted list, insertion does at most n shifts, usually far fewer, and uses no extra memory.

choices.text: Try every ordering and keep the sorted one
choices.feedback: That's n!, hopeless.

choices.text: It doesn't matter; both are the same Big-O here
choices.feedback: They're not: inserting one item is O(n) at worst, re-sorting is O(n log n).

exercises.title: When does the 'slower' algorithm win?
exercises.prompt: Algorithm P costs 50·n·log₂n operations; algorithm Q costs n². For n = 8, n = 64, and n = 1024, which is cheaper? Roughly where do they cross?
hints: Just compute both sides for each n. log₂ 8 = 3, log₂ 64 = 6, log₂ 1024 = 10.
The usual mistake is trusting the Big-O label ('n log n beats n²') without plugging in numbers. Big-O is about *large* n. The constant 50 matters for small n.
Set 50·n·log₂n = n² → 50·log₂n = n. Try n = 256 (log = 8 → 400 vs 256), n = 512 (log = 9 → 450 vs 512). The crossover is between them.
solution: n = 8: P = 50·8·3 = 1,200; Q = 64. Q wins by a mile.
Crossover where 50·log₂n = n: around n ≈ 450–500. Below it the quadratic algorithm is faster; above it, n log n pulls away forever.
exercises.why: This is exactly why Project 1's hybrid sort exists and why Java's own sort switches to insertion sort under ~47 elements. Engineers pick algorithms by measuring the crossover on real sizes, not by the label alone.

exercises.title: Trace merge sort in M() format
exercises.prompt: Trace merge sort on [9, 2, 7, 4, 1, 8, 3] in Poon's M([…]) format, indenting by depth and writing → result on every return. Left half gets the extra element.
hints: Write M([9,2,7,4,1,8,3]) at the top. Split: mid = (0+6)/2 = 3, so left is indexes 0..3 (four elements) and right is 4..6 (three). Indent each sub-call one level.

Two common slips: splitting so the *right* half gets the extra element (Poon's convention is left), and writing the merged result before both children have returned. Every → must come after both sub-calls above it.
Base case is a single element: M([x]) → [x] on one line. When you merge, do it with two fingers on paper: don't sort the two halves in your head.
solution: Seven elements, three levels of merging below the root: 7 × 3 ≈ 21 element-moves, matching n log n ≈ 7 × 2.8.
exercises.why: Merge sort is the algorithm behind external sorting (data too big for memory), behind `git merge`'s ordering, and behind Timsort in Python and Java. Being able to trace it means being able to debug a recursive function by hand: the skill that separates 'it works' from 'I know why'.

exercises.title: Why the temp array?
exercises.prompt: Try to merge the two sorted halves of [2, 5, 1, 4] *in place*, writing the merged output into the same four slots from left to right. Show the exact step where it breaks and explain what merge sort does instead and what that costs.
hints: Left half [2, 5], right half [1, 4]. Merge step 1: the smallest is 1. Where does it need to go? What's currently in that slot?

The mistake is to say 'just swap them'. Swap 1 and 2: [1, 5, 2, 4]. Now the right half is [2, 4]: still sorted, lucky: but keep going and you'll find swaps that break the sortedness of a half. Try [2, 6, 1, 3].
The clean argument: writing output to slot k overwrites an element you may not have read yet. So merge writes to a separate array and copies back: O(n) extra space, the price of O(n) merge time.
solution: Merge [2, 5] and [1, 4]: first output is 1, which belongs at index 0: but index 0 holds 2, which hasn't been placed yet. Writing 1 there destroys the 2.

Swapping instead of overwriting can break a half's sortedness in general (e.g. [2, 6, 1, 3]: after moving 1 to the front, the 2 lands in the right half ahead of 3: fine: but the next steps put 6 before 3).
Merge sort avoids this with a temp array: write the merged run into tmp[lo..hi], then copy back. Space O(n); time stays O(n) per merge.
Heap sort (Lecture 8) is the O(n log n) sort that manages without the extra array.
exercises.why: Memory is the constraint on phones, embedded devices, and GPUs. 'Does it need a copy of the data?' is one of the first questions asked about any algorithm in production, and the answer for merge sort is yes.
